raw_case_text:
A 20-year-old woman who recently emigrated from Mexico with limited prior medical care initially presented to an outside hospital with a facial rash thought to be herpes zoster with bacterial suprainfection. She was begun on a course of cephalexin and valacyclovir. Over the following week, she developed new-onset headache, emesis, and photophobia. After returning to the emergency department, she was found to have altered mental status which deteriorated further following a tonic-clonic seizure. A computed tomography scan of the head was unremarkable. Lumbar puncture demonstrated budding yeast and a cryptococcal antigen titer, performed by latex agglutination, that was greater than 1 : 256. During her hospitalization, she was found to be HIV-positive with a CD4 count of 10 cells/microL, a CD4/CD8 ratio of 7%, and an HIV viral load of 37,479 copies/mL.
The cryptococcal infection was initially treated with intravenous liposomal amphotericin 5 mg/kg daily and oral flucytosine 100 mg four times per day upon transfer. After fourteen days, the dose of liposomal amphotericin B was reduced to 4 mg/kg daily due to the onset of acute renal failure (creatinine 1.15 mg/dL from 0.60 mg/dL on admission). Antiretroviral therapy (ART) for HIV was withheld until completion of treatment of cryptococcal meningitis due to risk for immune reconstitution syndrome.
The patient clinically improved on this regimen, with complete resolution of meningeal symptoms within about one week of starting the antifungal regimen. However, soon afterwards, she developed worsening pancytopenia with prominent thrombocytopenia. Platelets were initially 144 k/microL and dropped to a nadir of 46 k/microL. Her white blood cell count decreased to a nadir of 1.8 k/microL (absolute neutrophil count 1100 cells/microL) from 3.4 k/microL and hemoglobin to a nadir of 6.5 g/dL from 9.3 g/dL. During this time, flucytosine was switched to fluconazole due to concern for precipitating worsening thrombocytopenia. Hematology consultation was obtained, and bone marrow aspirate and biopsy showed silver stain positive for disseminated Cryptococcus neoformans (Figure 1) with findings of focal phagocytosis, mildly hypocellular bone marrow for age (60% cellularity), and otherwise normal hematopoietic maturation with no evidence of malignancy. Additional negative studies of the bone marrow included acid-fast bacilli (AFB) stain and polymerase chain reaction (PCR) for Toxoplasma gondii, Cytomegalovirus (CMV), Parvovirus B19, and Bartonella. Histoplasma was not directly noted on histopathologic analysis of the bone marrow. The patient tested negative for CMV in the bone marrow but was positive for <1000 copies/mL of CMV in the peripheral blood. No treatment for CMV was administered.
Liposomal amphotericin B and fluconazole 800 mg daily were continued for a total of four weeks of induction therapy in the setting of Cryptococcus in the bone marrow and associated pancytopenia. Pancytopenia improved with continuation of this regimen. At the time of discharge to a long-term care facility, her white blood cell count was 2.4 k/microL, hemoglobin was 8.6 g/dL, and platelets had improved to 80 k/microL. The patient was started on abacavir/dolutegravir/lamivudine after two negative lumbar punctures. Given persistently elevated serum Cryptococcus Ag > 1 : 256, the patient was continued on suppressive fluconazole (200 mg daily) therapy for the next two years.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 20-year-old woman who recently emigrated from Mexico presented with a 1-week history of new-onset headache, emesis, and photophobia followed by altered mental status and a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, 1 week after presenting with a facial rash.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: One week after presenting to an outside hospital with a facial rash misdiagnosed as superinfected herpes zoster (treated with cephalexin and valacyclovir), the patient returned to the emergency department with 1 week of headache, vomiting, and photophobia, and rapidly deteriorated into altered mental status following a generalized tonic-clonic seizure.
subjective.past_medical_history: Recent immigrant from Mexico with limited prior medical care; newly diagnosed HIV infection during hospitalization.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for facial rash, headache, vomiting, photophobia, altered mental status, and tonic-clonic seizure. Recent medications: cephalexin and valacyclovir.

objective.physical_examination: Facial rash, altered mental status, and witnessed generalized tonic-clonic seizure.
objective.routine_investigations: HIV test was positive with plasma HIV viral load of 37,479 copies/mL; peripheral blood CMV PCR was <1000 copies/mL; serum creatinine rose from 0.60 mg/dL on admission to 1.15 mg/dL on day 14. Developed progressive pancytopenia during treatment: platelets dropped from 144 k/uL to a nadir of 46 k/uL (recovering to 80 k/uL at discharge), WBC dropped from 3.4 k/uL to 1.8 k/uL with ANC 1100/uL (2.4 k/uL at discharge), and hemoglobin dropped from 9.3 g/dL to 6.5 g/dL (8.6 g/dL at discharge). Serum cryptococcal antigen remained >1:256.
objective.advanced_workup: CD4+ T-cell count was 10 cells/uL (CD4/CD8 ratio 7%). Non-contrast head CT was unremarkable. Lumbar puncture CSF demonstrated budding yeast and a CSF cryptococcal antigen latex agglutination titer >1:256. Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy performed for pancytopenia revealed silver stain-positive disseminated Cryptococcus neoformans with focal phagocytosis and 60% cellularity, and negative bone marrow AFB stain and PCRs for Toxoplasma gondii, CMV, Parvovirus B19, and Bartonella.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of advanced HIV/AIDS with disseminated Cryptococcus neoformans infection involving the meninges, skin (herpes zoster-like facial rash), and bone marrow (causing pancytopenia), confirmed by CSF microscopy, CSF and serum CrAg latex agglutination titers >1:256, and bone marrow biopsy silver staining demonstrating C. neoformans with focal phagocytosis. Treated initially with IV liposomal amphotericin B (5 mg/kg/day, reduced to 4 mg/kg/day at day 14 for AKI) and oral flucytosine (switched to oral fluconazole 800 mg/day due to worsening thrombocytopenia) for a 4-week total induction course, resulting in resolution of meningeal symptoms and bone marrow recovery; ART (abacavir/dolutegravir/lamivudine) was started after two negative LPs, and she was discharged on suppressive fluconazole (200 mg/day for 2 years).
